summary:
Quinn Slack, CEO and co-founder of Sourcegraph (maker of code search and AI coding tool Cody), addresses the AI Engineer World's Fair with a thesis that should alarm the industry: despite enormous hype and investment, most developers worldwide still don't use code AI. He challenges inflated adoption statistics—GitHub's claim that 92% of devs use AI tools was US-only with a broad definition based on 500 respondents. Grounded numbers tell a different story: 1.3M paid Copilot subscribers, 935K yearly active users who merely received a suggestion, against an estimated 26M professional developers and possibly 100-150M people who touch code. His best-case estimate is ~5% of professional developers use code AI, mostly autocomplete.

Slack identifies adoption barriers: no compelling reason, wrong answers, company non-adoption, cost, and fading security/legal concerns. He maps the economic chain from foundation model companies through application builders to enterprises, estimating total code AI ARR at ~$300M, with Sourcegraph spending less than 10% of revenue on inference—meaning only ~$30M flows to model companies, 1/120th of Salesforce's $36B revenue.

Sourcegraph built Cody on 10 years of code search context, now #2 in revenue behind GitHub Copilot, with customers including 4 of the top 5 US banks. Early lessons: hype fools everyone, and autocomplete is a once-in-a-century feature. Slack warns that if your own team doesn't use the product daily, customers won't either. Customers asked for fine-tuned models but really just want products that work—if you can't describe why it's great without saying "AI," it won't make it. He poses an existential question: if the product makes devs 20-30% more productive, why not buy an outsourcing firm and monetize that value directly?

Slack introduces a feature evaluation framework: a 2x2 matrix of time-to-verify-correctness versus frequency of use. Autocomplete sits ideally top-right (instant verification, used every keystroke). Chat and inline edits are harder to vet and less frequent. Agentic code AI is the future but not yet real. Sourcegraph is searching for the next great modality, including chat-oriented programming (chop), where devs keep an ongoing chat session while coding. He advises building manual and explicit features first before adding magic, de-hyping aggressively when pitching (citing Sam Altman doing so with tens of millions of DAUs), and becoming a daily active user of your own product. He closes stressing ecosystem interdependence: foundation model companies, infra providers, and application builders all live or die together.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and the core thesis
sections.summary: Quinn Slack introduces himself as Sourcegraph CEO/co-founder and states his thesis: most developers still don't use code AI, which should scare everyone building AI products.

sections.title: Adoption statistics: hype vs reality
sections.summary: Slack dissects inflated adoption numbers. GitHub's 92% claim was US-only with broad definitions. Real numbers: 1.3M paid Copilot subscribers, 935K yearly active users who received a suggestion. Against 26M professional developers, best-case adoption is ~5%.

sections.title: Usage limitations and reasons for non-adoption
sections.summary: Most code AI usage is just autocomplete, not more powerful features. Reasons devs don't adopt: no good reason, unawareness, wrong answers, perceived lack of utility, company non-adoption, cost, and fading security/legal concerns.

sections.title: The economics of AI money flow and revenue
sections.summary: Slack traces money from foundation model companies through AI infra to application builders to enterprise customers. Total code AI ARR is ~$300M, with <10% flowing back to model companies (~$30M). This is 1/120th of Salesforce's $36B revenue.

sections.title: Sourcegraph background and first lessons
sections.summary: Sourcegraph built Cody on 10 years of code search context. Cody is #2 in revenue behind GitHub Copilot, with major enterprise customers. First lessons: hype fools everyone, and AI code completion is a once-in-a-century feature.

sections.title: Internal usage, customer delusion, and the existential monetization question
sections.summary: Slack warns that if your own team doesn't use the product daily, customers won't either. Customers asked for fine-tuned models but really just want products that work—if you can't describe why it's great without saying 'AI,' it won't make it. He poses an existential question: if the product makes devs 20-30% more productive, why not buy an outsourcing firm and monetize directly, rather than selling software?

sections.title: Feature evaluation framework and the autocomplete anomaly
sections.summary: Slack introduces a 2x2 matrix of time-to-verify-correctness versus frequency of use. Autocomplete sits ideally top-right (instant verification, every keystroke). Chat and inline edits are harder to vet and less frequent. Agentic code AI is the future but not ready—almost no one has merged a PR using an agent.

sections.title: Searching for the next great code AI modality
sections.summary: Sourcegraph is searching for the next autocomplete-level modality. Candidates include next-edit suggestions, chat-oriented programming (chop) where devs keep an ongoing chat session while coding, and other unimagined approaches. Build manual and explicit first—make context manually referenced, put agents in the editor so devs can fix errors directly—then add magic later.

sections.title: De-hype aggressively and become a DAU yourself
sections.summary: Always de-hype when pitching; even Sam Altman with tens of millions of DAUs sets expectations low, so builders should de-hype 10x more. Twitter hype doesn't translate to DAUs. Become a daily active user of your own product or kill it.

sections.title: Ecosystem interdependence and closing
sections.summary: Foundation model companies, AI infra providers, and application builders all live or die together. Model companies won't get paid unless applications generate real revenue. The ecosystem must collaborate, turn down hype, and build products devs use daily.

limitations: Adoption statistics may use broad definitions and limited geography, inflating perceived adoption
Number of developers touching code is estimated from informal 'Vibes citation' Google searches
GitHub reports yearly active users rather than monthly or daily, suggesting lower actual engagement
Market revenue estimates based on private internal information and conference-shared data
Productivity claims of 20-30% are self-reported by Sourcegraph and not independently validated
Audience hand-raise about agent PR merges is anecdotal, not a formal survey

~$30M flows back to foundation model companies from code AI

4 of top 5 biggest US banks are Sourcegraph customers
